title: Dynamic Thinking-Token Selection for Efficient Reasoning in Large Reasoning Models
claim: Prior cache-eviction methods keep tokens by fixed heuristics; ours keeps predicted decision-critical tokens, matching full accuracy with far less memory.
layout: 2 panels: left token-row comparison per method, right bar-line chart; ours highlighted
description: The left panel has three columns, labeled Methods, Tokens and Keeps. Five rows show Transformers, SnapKV, StreamingLLM, H2O and DynTS. Each row is a strip of small blocks followed by an ellipsis. Grey blocks are evicted tokens. Colored blocks are retained ones: orange for high-importance prefill tokens, yellow for attention sinks, green for heavy hitters, blue for local tokens, and red-orange for the tokens DynTS predicts as important. SnapKV has an observation-window bracket and a prompt bracket. In the DynTS row, curved arrows run from an 'Answer' bubble back to the retained tokens. A legend on the right explains the colors. The right panel is a bar chart of accuracy, with a dashed blue line for KV cache length on a second axis. Transformers and DynTS have the tallest bars, at 63.6 and 63.5, and DynTS is highlighted in red. The other methods are about 49 to 61. The KV line drops sharply for DynTS and stays low for the rest.
caption: (Left) Comparison of token selection strategies across different KV cache eviction methods. In each row, colored blocks denote the retained high-importance tokens, while grey blocks represent the evicted tokens during LRM inference. (Right) The average reasoning performance and KV cache memory footprint on DeepSeek-R1-Distall-Llama-8B and DeepSeek-R1-Distall-Qwen-7B across six reasoning benchmarks.
abstract: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) excel at solving complex problems by explicitly generating a reasoning trace before deriving the final answer. However, these extended generations incur substantial memory footprint and computational overhead, bottlenecking LRMs' efficiency. This work uses attention maps to analyze the influence of reasoning traces and uncover an interesting phenomenon: only some decision-critical tokens in a reasoning trace steer the model toward the final answer, while the remaining tokens contribute negligibly. Building on this observation, we propose Dynamic Thinking-Token Selection (DynTS). This method identifies decision-critical tokens and retains only their associated Key-Value (KV) cache states during inference, evicting the remaining redundant entries to optimize efficiency.
